utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I apologise, first of all, for the delay in starting caused by the efforts of the earlier sitting to complete the trial that started at 8.00 this morning. These efforts were successful, so in the end of the day I think the loss here is probably overall the Tribunal's gain. So I'm very grateful to you for your patience. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I asked if I could raise two brief matters before we resume with the witness. First of all, I want to introduce a new member of your team. Daniela Kravetz is sitting next to Mr. Stamp and will be assisting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, I wanted to raise with Your Honours the possibility of reading in 89(F) summaries for witnesses whom we introduce and use Rule 89(F) statements with. I've handed up and handed out to Defence counsel a proposed summary for the next witness to follow. It struck me that I think sometimes if we just bring in the witness and then we start to try and ask them questions, we're sort of starting out from a void. I believe you'll see that this is a very brief statement. If you compare it to the statement itself, I think you'll find it's accurate, it's entirely drawn from the statement, and I would ask you to reconsider that possibility, subject to any objections Defence counsel may have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I should express my own view of this. I consider this stage of a case as a time when evidence is given, not a time when people summarise other people's evidence, and I question the reason for doing it. If it's a public relations exercise just so that there's a summary for the public out there, then in my opinion that's not an appropriate exercise of the use of the courtroom. And as far as the Judges are concerned, they can read the statement, don't need a summary. So what's the purpose, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is partly a public relations matter in that we have an interest in having public trials here. We have expressed our interest in having as much of the proceedings as possible in open court. Some of the people watching this trial from outside, Your Honour, will not have the opportunity to see the written statements that go into evidence for these witnesses. And some of the people watching this trial, even if they could get their hands on the written copies of the documents don't read, frankly. So, Your Honour, this is an opportunity for them to hear what this 89(F) witness or the next 89(F) witness is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does any Defence counsel wish to comment on this issue? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recall that one of your reasons also for not wanting to proceed this way was because we don't want to enter into disputes over whether or not the summary read into court actually reflects what's in the actual 89(F) statement. And we certainly don't want to be putting ourselves in that situation, and there's a danger that that could happen. And we've received these summaries just before the witness enters and we'd be trying to see whether it accurately reflects or not the actual 89(F) statement. And that can lead to lots of dispute and time being wasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the other hand -- no, I entirely agree. I was accepting Mr. Hannis's assurance at the moment that the summary will be entirely accurate. But, Mr. O'Sullivan, yesterday -- now that I've had a chance to read Ms. Mitchell's statement, we simply had it explained to us yesterday in far greater detail than even the statement goes into. It was quite -- in my opinion, a quite unnecessary exercise or use of court time when that statement was readily available or could have been readily available for everyone to read. So, it's in a sense, commendable to think of a way of shortening the process by referring to a summary, but it just seems that -- to me that there must be a better way of doing it by asking a few focussed questions to identify what is the general nature of the witness's evidence. And I would have thought that skilled counsel should be able to do that without having to rely on a script which attempts to summarise the evidence. Now, is there any other comment to be made on the matter? Well, the Trial Chamber will consider the position and we'll make a ruling on it at a later stage, possibly today. But for the moment, just in case we don't make that ruling quite as quickly as you would like it, Mr. Hannis, you should be prepared to introduce the next witness through his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, before we continue with the evidence, I would like to ask -- to have certain things clarified. Mr. Stamp, we have the -- the principal statement for Ms. Mitchell for this case is a one-page statement which is -- was completed on the 8th of July, and it refers to a number of proposed exhibits. One is the agreement for the Kosovo Verification Mission, one is Resolution 1199, the third one is the report that's been challenged, and the fourth one is the Kosovo atlas 2 of maps. Now, is the last item there the large bundle of maps that we were handed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it something we haven't seen yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is something you haven't seen yet. But as it was referred to in the statement, it being a reference map really, it's something that might assist you in looking for locations. I didn't have an intention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how many maps of Kosovo do you intend to give us? I mean, Kosovo is not an enormous place, and we want to have this case simplified. It's the Prosecutor's challenge to make the case simple for the Judges. Now, why are you setting out to make it as complicated as you can on the surface, and why are you not content just to have one map or even one book of maps that we can work with?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm not actually setting out to make it complicated. The thing about it is that the map on this list is a map on the exhibits list that was filed. Some of the maps in the bundle are not on the exhibit list, but as it turned out when I had a look at the maps at some point in time, they seemed to me to be clearer, and it's a matter of opinion, than those on the exhibit list. So we are in a position where we would not want to -- to lose those maps which are not on the exhibit list. And we have a situation as well where we have not been able to agree any maps so far. I think we should be able to agree these maps. So until we can agree the maps and until the matter is settled and resolved, I think the Prosecution is just prudent to ensure that at the appropriate time it makes application to tender the maps which are on the exhibit list, just in case, out of an abundance of caution. Later on, the bundle might not be received or used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the Chamber is not in favour of admitting documents out of an abundance of caution. The Chamber is in favour of admitting documents that the Prosecution tendered to it that will be helpful to the Chamber in reaching its decision. And presenting more maps of Kosovo to us is, in our view, not helpful, and we are inclined to refuse to admit this bundle of documents and ask you to go back to the drawing-board with Mr. Hannis and sort out what maps you're going to rely on, because he's already given us a bundle, which is an expanded bundle of the Kosovo atlas. Now, as far as the other items are concerned, you did make reference in the course of the evidence to the Security Council resolution, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the agreement on the organisation. I now want to ask you just a few other points of clarification about this evidence. You say that there will be 12 witnesses who were people who provided information to the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they, I take it, relate to municipalities which are the subject of charges, either in -- set out in paragraph 72 or 75. You also said that there were roughly 2.800 documents, let's call them that, which recounted the experiences of people who either had made complaints of violent conduct or who were refugees explaining why they had moved. Are these 2.800 identified people?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the sense that they are named?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are the documents simply brief indications of their accounts rather than detailed statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are brief indications of their accounts. They are just a format -- the question is the format is in the bundle of documents, the format of the refugee questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was formulated by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it was formulated by the KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They formulated them. All right. And these are the documents you say that if the Defence asked to see them they would be permitted to see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They are not given to you under Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are given to us not -- they are given to us under the strictest confidentiality, not under Rule 70, but for use of the purposes of this case and other related cases. So the Defence would be entitled to see them, and we would make them available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Fila, it's for you -- sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You may not want to enter into this debate right now, but I would submit that there's more to this than just saying that they're available to us upon our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I expect you to make what submissions you wish to make on this issue when we decide -- or when you make submissions about the admissibility of the two volumes of the report. Mr. Fila, to continue with your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall continue, but I will not repeat the history because I finished with that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitchell, in your work you used local staff, especially interpreters and translators. Would you be able to tell us the ethnic composition of your local staff, i.e., who your interpreters were, how many of them were Albanians, how many of them were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Use of interpreters was -- included both Albanians, Serbians, Bosniaks, anybody in Kosovo. And how we used them depended on what the tasking was for that day. For example, it was dangerous to send Serbian interpreters to speak to the UCK. So Albanian interpreters would go, and then whether people knew the language, the exact numbers would have been -- again, depending on how many people are out in the field. Each international staff member would have been accompanied by an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I assume, for example, that maybe 90 per cent of your interpreters were Albanians? Would that be a fair assumption, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would have been that high. I think it would have been probably -- in our daily work we would be using 60 to 70 per cent because we would have been also dealing with the Serbian authorities, the VJ, and the MUP at the same time as part of ongoing activities, and there we would have been using the Serbian translators, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you don't mind, your answers can be even shorter to economise on time. What I would like to know now, since I understand that you are a lawyer by profession, did these interpreters have to take a solemn oath that they would interpret accurately, like our interpreters do here in the courtroom? Was that the case with your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They did take the oath?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They signed a confidentiality agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did not ask you that. I asked you whether they took the solemn oath; I didn't ask you about the confidentiality agreement. Here you took a solemn declaration that you would tell the truth. You did not sign an agreement that you would testify. As a lawyer, I believe that you see the difference, that you understand the difference. I believe my question was simple enough. I referred to an oath, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the confidentiality agreement, the person says that they will work honourably, translate correctly, et cetera. Did they take the same oath I took today? No, they did not, but there was an oath contained in the confidentiality statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand. It was a descriptive answer, but I understand. You were accommodated in houses and in hotels when you were engaged in your mission. In addition to Kosovo Polje, did you stay anywhere else on Kosovo in a house that was not owned by an Albanian? Can you give us an example of that, Kosovo as the whole region?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally have rented from both Albanians and Serbians during my time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you precisely. Save for Kosovo Polje, where else did you stay in a Serb house? If you can't remember, it's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure why you're putting me in Kosovo Polje. I lived in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm confused by the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect the assumption was that if you had been in Kosovo Polje you would have stayed in the house of a Serb, but elsewhere in Kosovo the likelihood is you would have stayed with an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because only Serbs lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since you were in Pristina, then perhaps you could explain whether you stayed with both in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, sir, during my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You stayed in Serb houses in Pristina and Kosovo Polje and elsewhere in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay in any houses in Kosovo Polje, but I stayed in -- I had a Serb apartment in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not ask about you personally. You had five places or points in Kosovo, not you personally but other people. It would not be appropriate for me to ask you where you personally lived. But your staff, where did they stay in Kosovo? And I'm not asking you at all about Kosovo Polje because Kosovo Polje is Serbian. So where did your staff stay in Kosovo, as a region?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't mean you personally.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. The KVM had offices in Pristina. It had regional offices in Pec/Peja, Gnjilane, Mitrovica, and Prizren. And then they had -- we had another 30-plus field offices in all of the opstinas, in the municipalities, including Kosovo Polje, Orahovac, Klina, Istok, Decan -- do you want me to name them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. I would like you to tell me at which of these places your staff stayed in Serb houses, if you know; if you don't know, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff would have stayed, usually for security reasons, would stay in -- if it was a Serb-dominated area, you rented the property from the Serbians; if it was an Albanian-dominated area, you rented from the Albanians. And so -- again, I can go through it municipality by municipality if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but I think the question is do you have direct knowledge of your staff staying in accommodation rented from Serbs? And if so, can you say in what areas that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have knowledge. It would have been in Mitrovica, in -- in the Strpci area, in the Gracanica area, in -- in Pristina, in Prizren, in Pec. Pretty much everywhere. We didn't distinguish upon ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understand you well, at places where the majority population was Albanian you stayed in Albanian houses; and where the majority population were Serbs, then you rented from the Serbs. Was my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I know -- and I want to clarify something from your statement. According to the SRY-OSCE agreement, the staff of your mission should have been unarmed and there should have been a plane that should have been used by your staff. Yesterday you told us that at one point in March, probably on the 22nd of March, 1999, you had to leave Kosovo for security reasons, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you were not armed. And when I say "you," I don't mean you personally, but all of you, all your staff, just to clarify this matter --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't make the same mistake again, counsel. That's correct, it was an unarmed mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who provided your security up to the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities responsible for Kosovo were also responsible for ensuring our security, and then there was a NATO extraction force that was put in place in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, only one member of your staff was injured by somebody from UCK. Correct me if I'm wrong. I believe that I'm right, though. Throughout your stay there, only one person was injured?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's my recollection, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you then leave Kosovo on the 22nd or the 24th? Who did you fear if your security was ensured by the Serbian authorities? If only one member of your staff had been injured, who did you fear? Why did you flee?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for the withdrawal was because of the increased presence of VJ, MUP, and additional security forces that were being deployed into Kosovo starting in larger numbers than we had seen in February -- January, February that year, and a continuing deterioration of the situation, military exercises occurring in Vucitrn, fighting in Kacanik, the displacement of the population. We were unable at that point in time to carry out our mandate, and we were concerned that the fighting was now escalating to a level that could not be contained and our staff were at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Two days later, NATO launched its first air-raid. Did you not know that? That is my question, actually. Were you aware of that fact? Did you leave Kosovo because you were not looking forward to NATO bombs?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We left Kosovo because the security situation was deteriorating as a result of the deployment and the conduct of the VJ and the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You did not have a clue then that NATO would start bombing Kosovo only two days later. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not privy to the operational plans of NATO, but I was obviously watching the news, like most people, and heard the political statements being made and the actions being taken in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We watch news as well. According to you, your mission continued its work from elsewhere. It was no longer in Kosovo and it is still operational. And what I'm going to ask you now is this -- let's go back to the incidents first. In your report you say that around 750 cases of violation of human rights were encountered and documented between October and March while you were there and that those incidents were never elucidated. My question is this: Is it correct that you had three representatives of the Yugoslav authorities, one who represented a federal government, that was General Loncar; the other one who represented the army, Colonel Kotur; and the third one, Mijatovic, who represented the MUP. And you had daily meetings with them, or almost daily meetings. And then you also had five main points where you had your liaison officers with the army and the police. And if all this is correct, my question is: How is it possible that you did not manage to elucidate so many cases, despite the number of people who were involved in that? I believe you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. We didn't get cooperation from our contact points in the VJ, the MUP, and the people that you referred to. We got very little cooperation from judges and prosecutors responsible for Kosovo. We got stonewalled in every investigation basically. Authorities do not admit to human rights violations and they hide evidence, and that's what was happening. And that made it very difficult to get to the bottom of many of the incidents that we were witnessing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand. In other words, you accept that you had daily meetings and contacts with the Yugoslav authorities. We agree on that, don't we, and those meetings were either in Pristina or on the ground. Did you report all of those incidents to them? That's my question and that is the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did report every incident as it was brought to our attention with the local officials and then up the chain of command, and daily meetings were occurring between KVM verifiers and all the authorities, including the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Yugoslav authorities when you reported those incidents?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was -- if it was an incident involving a man, the answer usually was: It was terrorism. These were terrorists. And the Yugoslav authorities had every right to deal with the situation in the way that they needed to, because they viewed pretty much all Albanian men as being members of the KLA, UCK, and called them terrorists. If it was incidents involving women, they were denied. And usually at that point in the conversation we were presented with evidence of crimes against Serbs and the discussion would then go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you remember perhaps that the verifiers discussed the incident in Kacanik with Colonel Kotur that even General Dijenkijevic went there with the investigating judge in Rogovo to see what had happened there. And let me remind you, a Serb policeman had been killed by UCK terrorists; that's what we referred to them at the time. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of an investigating judge in the Rogovo matter. Kacanik doesn't ring a bell, but that's just I can't remember. I don't deny that that would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now let me ask you something else. Yesterday I looked at your statement and I saw that once you left Kosovo you spent most of your time in Macedonia, Albania, and you worked with refugees there. And you told us that you did not go to Montenegro. Are you aware of the fact that some of the Albanian refugees fled to Crna Gora and to Serbia? Did you ever deal with these refugees? Did you ever try to get to the bottom of why they went to Montenegro and to Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were definitely aware of the flow of refugees in the directions of Montenegro and Serbia, but when the mission withdrew from Kosovo, Serbian authorities invalidated all of our visas and denied us access, either into Serbia or Montenegro. So we were unable to pursue those particular refugees, and they're not included in this documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And to this very day you have not included them? Is that what you're saying? Because the Milosevic regime was in place but is no longer. Like so many things, this has also come to an end.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mandate of the Kosovo Verification Mission ended when the NATO air campaign ceased and the agreement was reached to withdraw the forces. And so the mandate was gone, and I don't have anything to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's go back to the very beginning. During the time that you were there, between October and March, were you aware of the instances of kidnapping? At least a hundred Serbs had been kidnapped. Maybe you will not agree with the figure. Also some Albanians who were employed by the Yugoslav authorities had been kidnapped. And to this very day, it is not known where they are. There were killings, there were other things, and are these incidents equally represented in our reports, like all the other incidents? Because, if I may share my opinion with you, I would say that you are very selective. And there is another information from some 80 villages Serbs had been expelled, even before the NATO campaign started. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to all your questions contained in that bundle. I don't know the number of a hundred, but it doesn't matter. There were kidnappings of VJ officers by the UCK that I remember in December. That led to a complete breakdown in the cease-fire at that point. There were also kidnappings of Serbs that were being -- that were being reported, and we did follow up on those, sir, and they are included in the report. We tried as best we could to ensure that the -- all parties were living up to the standards, including the KLA, the UCK. And those instances, you're right, they haven't been solved. The issue of the missing is huge in Kosovo still, particularly for the Serbian population, and there needs to be answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question also included cases of Albanians who were working for the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there examples of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There are examples in the report of Albanians being beaten up, being detained illegally because they have a friend that may have been a police officer or a Serb or they had neighbours that they were friendly with. We were getting those reports as well, and those are also documented, and they were being brought to the attention of relevant UCK zone commanders at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this at the end. During the NATO campaign that we called aggression and you call NATO action, during the NATO action did Serbs leave Kosovo as refugees? Did you have information as to how many Serbs had left Kosovo as a result of NATO campaign?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- yes. We were receiving reports that -- of displacement from Kosovo cross the Brezova valley, into other parts of Serbia, internally displaced, not crossing an international border. We were also receiving reports of displacement within Kosovo, Serbians going to other Serb areas to feel safer. The numbers, as best one could determine, after the conflict when we went back in was it appeared as though there may have been as many as 100.000 Serbs that left Kosovo, but again numbers get very difficult in these issues. But those were the numbers that we were working with. It's gone up since then, I might add.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, this happened when NATO came. In percentages, how many Serbs left Kosovo? The 100.000 that you've mentioned, what would that be in percentage terms, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Court will indulge me just to tell you how we used the numbers. Population of Kosovo, based on a 1989 census that perhaps most Albanians may or may not have participated in, so a population of maybe 1.7, 1.9 for the Kosovo population at the time we're discussing, 90 per cent believed to be ethnic Albanians; of that number, the remaining 10 per cent are minorities, the largest minority -- and here we use the "minority" in quotes because we're talking about within Kosovo and not within Serbia proper, was about 10 per cent. So 10 per cent of the population, minorities. Of that -- you know, half of that would have been Serbian. Of that Serbian population, maybe half left. That's as -- that's as good as I can do on numbers without really having reference guides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these figures don't work, but it's at least an indication of a very large number or a large percentage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There remains in Kosovo approximately 124 or 125.000 Serbs now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me just make sure that I have not skipped something. I hope that you have spoken to some of these Serbs and asked them why they had left, either you or one of your verifiers. And this is my last question: Did any of these Serbs tell you that they were happy for being bombed? Do you have a case like that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of the Serbs that I've spoken to have said that they left because of -- they feared the NATO bombing They didn't have the same fear of the VJ and the Serbian police. And I don't recall anybody, not only in Kosovo, but anywhere telling me that they were happy to be bombed. I had no such cases, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I heard that yesterday about some other case. Well, in any case, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, I'm Norman Sepenuk, one of the attorneys for General Ojdanic. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As I understand it, a decision -- the decision was made to withdraw the KVM from Kosovo on March 20, 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made by Knut Vollbaek who was the chairman in office at the time for the OSCE and was the foreign minister of Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way, can you keep your voice up just a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What was the name of the gentleman who made the decision?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knut Vollbaek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you discuss -- You were the head of the human rights division. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you discuss that with him?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My reporting chain was to Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So when you said the -- when you gave us the reasons yesterday why you thought that the KVM left Kosovo, that was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the opinion -- that was the statements that were told to me by the head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You did speak to him then?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: To Ambassador Walker. And give us his role again?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker was the head of the Kosovo Verification Mission called -- his office is the head of mission, and he would have reported to Knut Vollbaek?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in answer to a question by Mr. Fila you said to -- as to whether you had a clue that NATO was going to be bombing just a few days later, you said: I was not privy to the operational plans of NATO, but I was obviously watching the news like most people and heard the political statements and the actions being taken in Brussels. And if you saw it I take it your superiors saw it, too?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So are you stating -- and I'm just asking. Are you stating categorically that the NATO bombing played no part whatsoever in the OSCE-KVM decision to leave?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. I'm saying that the security situation resulted in the mission leaving, and the fact that NATO was planning to intervene was an indication of the seriousness of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I want to ask a few questions about the refugee monitoring forms used by OSCE personnel in interviewing refugees who came to Albania and Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And would the usher be good enough to post Prosecution Exhibit 765.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you. We don't have it on our screen here. Perhaps there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now we have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was -- if you -- do you immediately recognise this --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- as the form that was used?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This was the form that was used by the OSCE investigators in both Albania and Macedonia. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you'll note --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher would just scroll up a bit. You can stop right there -- no. Stop right there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the first question is: "Describe the situation in the last place of residence," and underneath that: "(a), circumstances of departure/reasons for flight." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, did the -- your investigators have these forms in-hand, I take it, when they were interviewing the Albanians. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And were they filling them out as the Albanians were speaking? I take it your investigators were writing down what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And these forms, after they were filled out, tell us what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forms would have been filled out in refugee camps or in vehicles. They were collected -- the way the field operation was is we had teams going into the camps, and so there was a team leader, and the team leader at the end of the night collected all of the statements. Depending on how close the particular site -- location of the staff was to either Tirana, Albania, Skopje, Macedonia, they were then delivered each night to either me or my deputy in either of those offices. At that time -- and if that wasn't the case, then they were brought in every three or four days when somebody was going to be capitals, which was frequent. At that point, they were numbered and one photocopy was made. The document -- the original document was put in -- was put in a binder and then immediately transferred to ICTY, to the Prosecutor's office, on a daily basis. And the copies were put in similar binders and kept in Skopje and in Tirana until such time that they were all then relocated to Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was furnished to the Prosecutor then, as I understand it, was this Exhibit 765?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the completed documents, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In the handwriting of the investigator?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the OTP would get it on virtually a -- would get it on virtually a daily basis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were there forms then -- were there other forms -- and by the way, I take it you felt that this was confidential?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And the last question on the questionnaire is an authorisation, a consent, to share the information with ICTY. And it was always locked up. We found it extremely -- we thought it was very sensitive information in a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was the OTP the only group that received these statements?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the only ones that received the statements. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights had an office in Skopje, and ICRC could look at the statements if there were issues relating to either of their specific mandates. But they were not given copies ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Nor were the other -- nor were, I take it, other organisations be given copies, like the Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is there a group called the International Crisis Group?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And where are they based?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're based in Brussels. There was a whole lot of people collecting statements. We kept them out of our process completely. We were aware it was going on, but their information was not incorporated into ours, and at no time did we ever share the information with ICG or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you can help us out with something. Last night --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I'll address this to Your Honours -- and forgive the choppiness for the next few minutes. We received from the OTP about 6.00 last evening something called an interview full report. And as a matter of fact, to clarify this, if the witness could be shown -- incidentally, Your Honour, we just discovered this last night and we only found out certain other things this morning. So we apologise for not having it in the e-court proceedings. But if the witness could be shown what we have marked as defendant exhibit 3D00-001 and also D00-002, and we have copies for the Prosecutor and the panel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In other words, these are documents 1 and 2, right? I think we can do without the 0000s when we're trying to identify these. One will do for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 1 and 2 it shall be, Your Honour, from here on out. I promise. And copies for the panel, please. Now, do Your Honours have copies now? And perhaps you can put defendant exhibit 1 on the ELMO, that might take care of it for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you see that document in front of you, which is defendant exhibit 1?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a print-out from a database that was developed in Warsaw to try to manage the volume of information so that it could be more easily accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So is -- and who prepared that document?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who prepared this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Who would have prepared a document like that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would have prepared it? There was a team of six to eight people that we had in Warsaw working on the refugee statements in the KVM, and one of them or somebody from that staff would have entered that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the information on this form, i.e., defendant exhibit 1, would have come from Prosecution Exhibit 765 that we looked at first?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And would you now look at -- and by the way, before we leave that, you'll notice on -- it's K0529763, it's the next page, it talks about what happened. "Mass Serb police with painted faces, soldiers, and paramilitaries forced the witness and other villagers out of their houses." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm reading correctly?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you look at defendant exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if the usher would simply put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this is what we need your help on, and we're asking just for clarification purposes. What is that document?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it has ICG's name on it, so I'm assuming it's from the ICG database that they would have developed based on a template that was being used in the field at the time by many of the organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that's -- the ICG is the International --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crisis Group. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And can you notice what it says there about what happened? It seems to be word for word the same.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And frankly, you know -- what's the explanation?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, people were getting interviewed -- this was a huge problem in the field. People were getting interviewed and re-interviewed. Sometimes we had organisations sort of following around our staff to conduct additional interviews of people for their own mandated problems and issues, and it was very frustrating. It was very, very difficult to manage. And it was, at times, a problem. I'm not saying that this particular case is one of those, but we also had reporters following our staff around in the camps as well because they thought that we had the best witnesses, and it's -- I'm not surprised to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, when you say you're not sure whether this particular case is one of them, maybe I'm truly missing the point here.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But the ICG defendant exhibit 2, the description of the incident and the reason for leaving is word for word the same as the OSCE description. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The documents speak for themselves, and I've given the best explanation I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So is the only conclusion that one -- that we can draw from this is that somehow the ICG was privy to your information?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've stated, we had the measures in place to ensure as best as we could the security and the confidentiality of the information. There were a lot of people following and getting statements. People were working together. The rule was, you know, the information was only being shared with ICTY, and if, you know, somebody breaks the rule, they break the rule. But it -- it -- that's as much as I can say on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So what you're saying here is that at least based on what you're saying it appears that one of your investigators shared information with the International Crisis Group, against the rules of your organisation?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility. It's also that possibility that this person re-interviewed somebody that we had interviewed and came up with the same story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Word for word?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I -- that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything's possible. I've given you, you know, the reasons that I can think of as honestly as I can. And if they shared a form, they shared a form, and, yeah, the rule was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I won't belabour it, Your Honour, but I have two other exhibits, exhibits 3 and 4, which make the same points, and we would tender those also as exhibits. It's the same process, Your Honour, of word-for-word repetition, the ICG repeating in its form word for word what the OSCE's form says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Sepenuk, what you should do is ask the witness to identify the other documents without going into the detail of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then we've got numbers for them, presumably, as well, and that rectifies any deficiency in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So if you would simply give the witness defendant exhibits 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you look at defendant exhibits 3D3 and 3D4, and is it fair to say that that represents the same process that I just questioned you about, only with respect to another person?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now I want to turn to another aspect. As I understand it, the conclusions in your report, As Seen, As Told, which was Prosecution's Exhibit 473 is based on some 27 to 2800 refugee interviews by the OSCE. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And those were refugees in Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it further, there were thousands of interviews that took place in Albania and Macedonia of refugees. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thousands?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would be quite that high.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But what? If you had -- if you had to give us your best estimate?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the largest number -- I honestly don't know how many the other organisations would have interviewed --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I think that's too high. I would think under 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The figure was given to us yesterday by one of the Prosecutors, tens of thousands, do you think that might be a little too high?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. If you throw in the journalists and researchers and others, my number refers to those that may have been actually involved in collecting this type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So these are thousands of interviews over and above the 27 and 2800 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, the figure given by one of the Prosecutors yesterday referred to refugee data forms, not just taken in Albania and Macedonia, but taken generally in respect to Kosova by international organisations or governments, which the witness would not know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So are these 27 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. My recollection yesterday was the expression -- yeah, you -- the statement you made yesterday, Mr. Stamp, was that there were tens of thousands of forms that were not made available on the electronic disclosure system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. In other words, I am saying that the statement I made yesterday, unless I am mistaken, and I'm sure I could be corrected, did not restrict the provenance of the forms to Montenegro and Albania, which is the way the question is phrased now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll ask another question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, you may want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The ELMO is not going to be needed any more, so you might want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just so there's no doubt about it, am I correct in my understanding that the OSCE itself conducted thousands of interviews?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Over and above the 27, 2800? There were 2700, 2800 refugee interviews that the As Seen, As Told was based on, but you're saying that there was also thousands of interviews over and above that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I answered your question of whether the OSCE conducted thousands of interviews, I'm including the 27, 2800 figure. In addition to that, I would say you're looking at maybe 1.000, 1500 that would potentially have involved people that were met, briefed, but then statements weren't taken for whatever reasons. It would be that type of an activity, much briefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So when you testified yesterday that there were thousands of refugee interviews, which you did. I can refer you to the statement, if you'd like. And when you testified in your statement twice, or at least your submitted statement, that there were thousands of interviews, and when you testified at the Milosevic trial that there were thousands of Albanians interviewed, are you saying that you only meant another 1.000, 2.000 above the 27, 2800?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I always included those numbers in the word "thousands."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So all you meant there were 3300, 4.000 interviews? Give us your best judgement, please.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that would probably be about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That would be about right. That's what you meant by "thousands"?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's "thousands" to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Just asking. And do you have a record of all those interviews? Were all of those interviews submitted to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And tell us how that came about.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oftentimes you would talk to a group of people and you may get so far in the interview and for a variety of reasons, they didn't directly see something, you come quickly that they're talking about a story three other people may have told. So it stops, and there's nothing written down. Also, when we evacuated, a lot of the information we were unable to bring out for purely logistical reasons. And so those would have been destroyed at the time. So that's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are the 750 complaints of violence, are they included in the 2.800 roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They are in addition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So I take it that other than the 2700 or so that's been turned over to the OTP, there doesn't exist to your knowledge any record of these other interviews, whether it's 1500, 2.000, whatever the amount is?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, but I don't know the exact number. But we did also turn over the files that we evacuated from Kosovo for the period from October to March, whatever was evacuated, and I honestly don't remember how many statements were in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Who did you turn that over to?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- it's also been incorporated into this report and they would have -- it would have been turned over to ICTY -- excuse me, to the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And that's for what period, just so I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The files, as soon as we began. So from October or November until March, to the withdrawal of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You mean June?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: March. Okay. It didn't cover interviews after that? Because we're talking about March, April, May, June, the entire period --

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure I understood, but let me just try to clarify. Between the period of October and March, there was documentation that was collected in Kosovo that is included in the report. Some but not all of that documentation was withdrawn with us. That was subsequently part of the analysis for the preparation of the report, and then it was turned over for the period from the evacuation in March through June would have been the refugee statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And those -- any refugee statements you did make a record of was turned over to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to go back to the distinction between these two groups of reports. The 750 roughly incidents of violence, are they contained in the October to March batch or are they spread over that and the later period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 750 figure that we're discussing is the October to March batch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that roughly the number of files or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or is there no relationship between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That 750 would have been incident reports that would have been completed. And those that were more specifically developed we would have evacuated. If we didn't have enough, we destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, I just want to talk briefly or ask you briefly about the OSCE relationship with the Albanian refugees who came from Kosovo to Albania and Macedonia. Tell us the role of that bright orange car that you spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the mission was first deployed in October of 1998, vehicles were moved from the missions in Bosnia and the region to jump-start the operation, and they were all white. At the time these were Pajeros, and at the time the MUP were driving white Pajeros. So it became a security issue because the KLA often shot at the MUP, and we didn't want them shooting at us, so we painted the cars a colour that could be -- without distinction people would know who it was as a security measure, so they were painted this bright fluorescent orange colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that was sort of symbol or that was part of your entree, was it not, into the Albanian community. When they saw that bright orange car, they knew it was OSCE people?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, all the communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as I think you've testified before, that gave you sort of an entree again into the community so you can talk to them, find out what happened to them, find out about their welfare, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this was symbolic in that it opened up dialogue and lines of communication with the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that you - and I mean the OSCE-KVM - had a very special relationship with the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the refugee camps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it's also fair, I take it to say, that you didn't have a very special relationship with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a special relationship; it was just a different kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, you didn't cover in your report why the Serbs left Kosovo during the NATO air campaign, did you?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report we discussed why communities throughout Kosovo left. There are reports of what happened to some of the Serbians in the villages as they were being recounted to us by refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. But again, there was nothing specifically in the report as there was about the Albanians as to why the Serbs left Kosovo during the NATO air campaign?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have access to the Serbs. They didn't come to Albania or Macedonia, and so we were not able to access them, which is the reason for the -- that they're not included. It was an access issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So I take it the answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, though, that there -- we -- the report does cover the effects of some of the Serbians. And in that context, there may be explanations as to why they left. So I'm -- I just -- I know what you're trying to get me to agree to, and I'm just uncomfortable with it, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to agree to anything that's not so. And let me refer to your testimony in Milosevic case, if I might. Page 7543 of 5 July 2002. And at that time you said, and I quote that: "As far as the reasons why the Serbs left Kosovo during the NATO air campaign, I would have to refer you to other human rights organisations that had access and documented that -- documented that at the time. It's just not covered in our reports, unfortunately." Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, finally I'd like to turn to the relationship between the OSCE and the OTP of the ICTY during the period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you were the primary liaison of the OSCE to the OTP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And all of the information -- is it fair to say that all of the information gathered by your group, in essence, was turned over to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just during the particular period of the refugee situation, not during the period of October to March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. But any information regarding alleged violations of international humanitarian law was indeed turned over to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And of course you obviously furnished a copy of your report immediately to the OTP? That's Prosecution Exhibit 473, As Seen, As Told?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, Justice Louise Arbour wrote the forward to that report, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was Justice Louise Arbour's position at that time? This was in 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was her position at that time?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she was still the Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: She was the lead Prosecutor here, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that's the same Justice Arbour who signed the initial indictment in this case in 1999 against three of these defendants. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Aleksic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Since I'm the fifth, a number of questions have already been asked. But now I only need to manage my resources better. Therefore, the number of questions I have will be less than that of my colleagues, and I will do as best I can not to repeat any of the topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I am counsel for General Lazarevic. In your statement dated the 2nd of July, 2002, you state that the refugee monitoring plan was put together by you personally and that you did so two days after the 22nd of March of -- rather, on which date the verification mission withdrew from Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show us Exhibit P764.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is this the plan of monitoring refugees that we just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First I'd like to clarify something concerning the refugee monitoring plan that was dated the 22nd of March. And in your statement you said you drafted the plan two days after the 22nd of March when the verification mission left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we left Kosovo on March 20th, and I think this document is dated March 22nd, is it? I can't see the second page, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, the 22nd of March. Hence my question, Mrs. Mitchell, is the following: Why did you make the refugee monitoring plan as late as the 22nd of March of 1999 once you had left Kosovo? Why hasn't it been put together earlier?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very busy in Kosovo and focussing at that point on trying to document as much as we could while we were there. We -- it was overwhelming once one realised that the population was going to be expelled, and the events on the ground drove the development of the refugee monitoring plan. It was not something that was contemplated at the time that we were in the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that before the 22nd of March, 1999, you were very busy with more emergency or immediate tasks than to monitor refugees, or is my interpretation incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have the refugees at that time. We had displacement, yes, and displacement was increasing, but we didn't have the refugees and we weren't there. We were inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That means that you thought that with the initiation of NATO air strikes and after you leave Kosovo there would be an influx of refugees in the surrounding areas, and that's why you created this monitoring plan?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We created the monitoring plan because we were evacuated to Skopje, and shortly thereafter large numbers of people started pouring over the borders telling us atrocious things, and we needed a way to manage that particular activity and continue the mandate. It was driven by the events that were happening. My job was to react at the operational level, and that's how the plan was developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That is clear, but you created this plan on the 22nd of March. At that time there was -- there were no refugees in great numbers. And in your statement on that date, you state that in Macedonia there were 8.000 refugees, and in Albania 18 and a half thousand. You made this plan before the mass exodus began?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The people were already leaving Kosovo, sir, and had been for several weeks and months prior to the evacuation because of ongoing security actions by the VJ and the MUP. Shelling villages in Kacanik was creating a flow into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well. Since that was so, why did you make this plan as late as the 22nd of March? Why hasn't it been created earlier once you established that there were great numbers of refugees moving towards Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operational mandate for the Kosovo Verification Mission was in the province, the territory, of Kosovo. When we left, the mandate continued -- the human rights mandate continued insofar as talking to people from Kosovo that were now in Macedonia and in Albania. We didn't do it beforehand because we weren't physically located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It means that for as long as you were physically in Kosovo there were no representatives of yours in Albania and Macedonia whatsoever? Are you trying to tell me that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were representatives. The OSCE had missions, separate missions, in Albania and in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, but we didn't have our human rights staff deployed there until after the withdrawal of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitchell, correct me if I'm mistaken, but the Prosecution exhibit you have before you speaks of the strengthening of the mission rather than its establishment on the 22nd of March. Since it mentions the increase in numbers, then it must have existed previously. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're -- this particular proposal was discussing strengthening the already existing OSCE missions in Albania and in Macedonia that had separate mandates, to augment those missions with our staff because we were not operational at that time in those areas. Did that clarify, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does that mean they had nothing to do with you?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the withdrawal of the mission, no, they had independent mandates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: These independent mandates, did it mean that they had no right to monitor refugee movement, to speak to them, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the OSCE field missions have a human rights mandate for anybody in the territory where their mandate continues. And so if it was a refugee situation, they would fall under the human rights general mandate for every mission. But they certainly didn't have the capacity to respond to the influx and the numbers that were pouring over the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: They didn't speak to those refugees because of their lack of personnel prior to your withdrawal from Kosovo. Are you trying to tell me that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say that. They may have been speaking to the refugees that were coming over in the months that we were there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you say "maybe," Mrs. Mitchell, I would be most interested in finding out whether you have such information or a document that would confirm that, since you say that later on you formed a joint mission. Perhaps this is merely an assumption on my part, but have you ever encountered a document or a statement taken prior to your withdrawal from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the mission in Macedonia subsequently, and I know in looking through some of their historical files that they were reporting on the influx in the months prior to the withdrawal of the mission. So they're in their weekly reports, but I don't know that I've ever seen any specific statements in that regard along the lines of the forms that we've been discussing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That means that the statements were taken without any control on your part and without any direction or instruction that was created later on, as late as the 22nd of March? There was no procedure in place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I must say I'm not following this at all. I don't understand the line you're pursuing. The witness has told you that in Macedonia and Albania there were no human rights offices at the time prior to the beginning of the influx. And while they had a general human rights mandate, there was no system for recording the accounts of these and that she set up the system when the human rights officers moved from Kosovo and were available in Albania and Macedonia. Now, is there something else that you're trying to establish from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I simply wanted to clarify something, and perhaps I will manage to do so with my next question. Mrs. Mitchell, in her statement and in her testimony yesterday, stated that there were 200 people who were supposed to work with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When were they employed? Out of that number, 75 were in Albania, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a group that came from the larger 1300 that were evacuated. Many were sent home, and then the mission shrunk down to around 450 total, is the best of my recollection, of which 200 were assigned to these particular tasks, and 75 in Albania, 125 in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And they had specific duties after your withdrawal from Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned - and it is also mentioned in your statement - that those were mostly trained people. But if I understood correctly, you said that you would allow for a possibility that some of them were untrained as well?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 200 that you're talking about were sort of the cream of the crop, so these were the more highly trained of the larger mission complement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Didn't you state yesterday that you carried out training for some people? When was that?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that period that we're talking about, counsel, was the period from probably November to early March, the type of training which we tried to do throughout the mission. During the withdrawal, the training strictly focussed then on interviewing techniques and management of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm afraid we'll have to interrupt you. I've been allowing this to go beyond the allotted time, thinking that you just had a brief cross-examination. But since it's obviously going to take some time, we'll interrupt it now, and we will resume at quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready to continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mrs. Mitchell, just before the break, if I'm not mistaken, you said that during the withdrawal the training concerned with -- data processing and interviewing refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me what it meant "during the withdrawal." Does that mean that the training was conducted once you were in Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah -- sorry. The trainings were conducted as teams were being deployed and the operations were being set up in Macedonia and in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I understand. Mrs. Mitchell, since you said that the mission shrank and that you brought 200 people who were the best of the group, why would such people require additional training?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL [Resumed]
